question: A 6-month-old infant male is brought to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of vomiting and convulsions. He was born at home and had sporadic prenatal care though his parents say that he appeared healthy at birth. He initially fed well; however, his parents have noticed that he has been feeding poorly and is very irritable since they moved on to baby foods. They have also noticed mild yellowing of his skin but assumed it would go away over time. On presentation, he is found to be very sleepy, and physical exam reveals an enlarged liver and spleen. The rest of the physical exam is normal. Which of the following enzymes is most likely functioning abnormally in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Galactokinase deficiency -> Accumulation of galactose -> Galactitol formation -> Liver and spleen enlargement -> 95%
enhanced_information: In this case, the most likely enzyme functioning abnormally in the patient is Galactokinase deficiency. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of galactose, which can further result in galactitol formation. The enlargement of the liver and spleen observed in the patient is consistent with this pathway. The evidence path mentioning Salmonella typhimurium is not directly relevant to the patient's presentation and can be disregarded.
analysis: The patient's presentation with vomiting, convulsions, irritability, feeding difficulties, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly is suggestive of galactokinase deficiency. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of galactose and subsequent galactitol formation, explaining the observed symptoms. Aldolase B deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance) typically presents with hypoglycemia, vomiting, and hepatomegaly but does not involve galactose metabolism. Fructokinase deficiency leads to essential fructosuria, which is typically benign. Gal-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency causes classic galactosemia, presenting with failure to thrive, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and cataracts. Lactase deficiency results in lactose intolerance, typically manifesting with gastrointestinal symptoms after milk ingestion.
